title: Six pairs
hookLine: calm, lightness, softness, workability, skill and straightness, in body and in mind

cards: Cold dough tears. Push a rolling pin across it straight from the fridge and it cracks at the edges, fights back, springs into its old shape.
Leave the same dough on the counter for a while and it rolls out smooth, takes any shape, does what the hands ask. Nothing was added. It just softened.
Today the manual finishes its list of the beautiful factors with six qualities that sound a lot like warm dough.

teach.h: ONE OF THE BODY, ONE OF THE MIND.
teach.b: The six come in pairs, and every pair has the same shape: one of the body, one of the mind. Tranquility, passaddhi: calm, the settling of agitation. Lightness, lahuta: not heavy, not dragging.
Softness, muduta: not rigid, not stubborn. Workability, kammannata: fit for work, ready to be used. Proficiency, pagunnata: skill, a mind that runs well.

And straightness, ujukata: not crooked, without twists or tricks. A note on body. In the Abhidhamma, the body in these pairs means the cluster of mental factors, the mind's own small body, not flesh and bone.
Still, some teachers point out that these qualities can be felt physically too, in shoulders that drop, a jaw that lets go. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha describes gold being refined.
Iron, copper, tin, lead and silver are worked out of it, and then the gold is pliant, workable and bright, ready for whatever ornament the goldsmith has in mind.
So too, he says, a mind freed of its impurities is pliant, workable and luminous.

Straightness has a Dhammapada verse of its own, in Max Müller's words: "As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back."
Here's the useful part. In the manual, these qualities aren't a prize at the end of a long road.
They're counted in every beautiful moment, so whenever kindness or clear seeing happens, some softness and workability are already in it.
On this account, a stiff, stubborn mood can't arise in the same moment as real generosity.

teach.h: COLD DOUGH, OR DOUGH THAT ROLLS.
teach.b: One is cold dough. The other rolls.

how: Abhidhamma students learn the six pairs as part of the beautiful factors, and some meditation teachers point to tranquility, lightness and pliancy of body and mind as signs that practice is settling.

o: calm, lightness, softness and more, each in body and mind

games.q: soft and workable: tap the pairs.

s: in these pairs, 'body' means flesh and bone
in the Abhidhamma it means the cluster of mental factors, though some teachers note it can be felt physically too.
the Buddha compares a mind freed of impurities to refined gold
worked free of iron, copper, tin, lead and silver, gold is pliant, workable and bright.
in the manual, these qualities appear only after long practice
the manual counts them in every beautiful moment.

games.q: you're a goldsmith. the gold in your crucible is brittle and dull, mixed with iron and tin. what do you do?
o: keep refining until it's pliant and bright.
polish the outside so it looks bright.
games.why: in the Anguttara Nikaya, the goldsmith works out iron, copper, tin, lead and silver, and then the gold is pliant, workable and bright. the Buddha says a mind freed of its impurities is the same.

practice: If you'd like, go looking for stiffness, the jaw, the shoulders, the hands, the space between the eyebrows, without forcing anything to relax.
Rest attention there, let the next out-breath be a little longer, and see if the place softens on its own, the way dough does on a counter.
Then check the mind the same way, and if it's gripping a thought stiffly, let it be held a little more lightly.

wordCard.voice: Six pairs. Calm, lightness, softness, workability, skill and straightness, each in the body of mental factors and in the mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali passaddhi: tranquility, the first of the six pairs.

carryVoice: Your line: soft and workable. Like refined gold: pliant, and ready. See you tomorrow.
